title: The body's nature
hook: art students draw the skeleton before the skin. some monks went further. two views on why, and how carefully.
tomorrow: is a practice like that meant to make you hate bodies?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sign appears: the object taken in so well it stays with eyes closed, then a purer sign, to be guarded. Today a harder subject, and two careful views of it.

Art students learn to draw the skeleton before the skin; a figure looks wrong until you know what's holding it up. Monks in the old texts went further. The Satipatthana Sutta describes a monk at a charnel ground, where bodies were left in the open, looking at one over time: newly dead, then picked at by birds, then a skeleton, then scattered bones, then dust. Each time, he turns back to his own body and reflects: this body too is of that nature. It will become like that. Which is yesterday's question: why would anyone meditate on a skeleton?
screen: `THE SKELETON BEFORE THE SKIN.` → `A CHARNEL GROUND.` → `THIS BODY TOO IS OF THAT NATURE.`

segments.voice: Buddhaghosa gives the answer a whole chapter: ten foulness subjects, asubha, the stages of a body after death, from swollen to a scatter of bones. They're medicine, he says, for one temperament in particular, the greedy one, the mind that clings to looks and lust. And here two views open up. The first says: keep it, plainly. The Buddha taught it himself. Its best case: people cling to bodies, their own and other people's, as if they'll stay young and lovely forever, and one honest look loosens that grip faster than any argument. A practice isn't wrong just because it's uncomfortable. The second says: handle with great care. Its best case comes from the manual itself. Buddhaghosa says to go only with a teacher's permission, to tell a senior monk where you're going, to mind the time and the direction of the wind, and he matches the subject to a temperament, not to everyone. The same Buddha gave other people kindness, or the breath. Medicine without the right dose can do harm. What neither side disputes is the sutta's line: this body too is of that nature. Not a threat. A fact, held calmly: the body changes.
screen: `TEN STAGES, FOR ONE TEMPERAMENT.` · `KEEP IT: ONE LOOK LOOSENS THE GRIP.` · `CAREFUL: A TEACHER, THE RIGHT DOSE.` · `BOTH AGREE: THIS BODY CHANGES.` · then, large: `THE BODY CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Look at one of your hands for a while: the lines, the knuckles, a scar if there is one. Bring to mind how it looked when you were small, and how it may look when you're old. Rest in that plainly, without picturing anything grim: this hand changes.
Asubha: the unlovely, or foulness. Stages of a body after death, held as a meditation subject, with a teacher.
Your line: the body changes. Both sides of the debate agree on that much. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada tradition the foulness meditations are taught to some monks and lay practitioners by a teacher, matched to temperament; the charnel-ground reflections of the Satipatthana Sutta are recited and studied more widely.

fork.setup: your meditation group debates whether foulness practice belongs in a beginners' class. you lean toward leaving it out. state the other side's best case.
options: it's shocking, and the shock alone is what keeps people awake.
the Buddha taught it, and one honest look loosens the grip of looks.
people long ago saw death all the time, so it felt normal then.
fork.reveal: that's the strongest version: the Buddha's own teaching, and an honest look at change. the careful side's best case is real too: the manual says a teacher, and the right temperament.

original.note: Pali: unlovely, not beautiful; usually rendered 'foulness'. The ten stages of a body after death as meditation subjects.

what a scholar hears: the ten foulness subjects of Visuddhimagga 6, rooted in the charnel-ground reflections of MN 10: this body too is of that nature.

chat.says: art class anatomy week: drawing skeletons under the skin for the mural figures. kinda grim? or useful?
options: Useful, if you keep it calm: bodies change, and seeing what's underneath is honest.
Grim. Buddhism says the body is disgusting, so you're supposed to hate it.
Useful for art only. The Buddha never asked anyone to think about bones.
chat.meaning: The sutta's line is calm: this body too is of that nature. Seeing what's underneath is about change, not disgust.

tie.story: The charnel-ground monk reflects calmly: this body too is of that nature.
tie.friend: Mai's skeleton sketches can be honest about bodies without being grim.
tie.you: what about your own body has already changed, and how do you feel about that?

charnel ground.meaning: a place where bodies were left in the open

Satipatthana Sutta.meaning: the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness

Buddhaghosa.meaning: the commentator who wrote the Path of Purification

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 10 (Satipatthana Sutta, the charnel-ground contemplations: a body one day dead … eaten by birds and animals … a skeleton … bones scattered … crumbled to dust; 'this body too is of the same nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that')
Visuddhimagga 6 (the ten foulness subjects, the bloated to the skeleton; suited to the greedy temperament; go with a teacher's permission, inform a senior monk, mind the time and the wind direction)

notes: Gentle note for parents: this day touches death and the stages of a body after death. The script stays non-graphic (it names only 'swollen' to 'a scatter of bones', and the sutta's 'picked at by birds … dust').

Debate shape: 'keep it, plainly' vs 'handle with great care'. Both views are drawn from inside the tradition (the Buddha's teaching in MN 10; Buddhaghosa's own cautions in Visuddhimagga 6); neither is ranked, and both agree on the sutta's line. Confirm.
MN 10 paraphrased (no PD translation quoted). The stages given are a shortened selection. Confirm 'this body too is of that nature; it will become like that'.
Visuddhimagga 6 paraphrased: ten subjects; suited to the greedy temperament; the cautions (teacher's permission, informing a senior monk, time and wind direction). Confirm.
'The same Buddha gave other people kindness, or the breath' points to Udana 4.1 / AN 9.3 (Meghiya), used more fully on day 1523.
